result: The vast majority (95.2 ± 0.3%) of ChR2-eYFP-expressing SuM boutons in the DG co-expressed both VGluT2 and VIAAT, confirming that SuM terminals contain both glutamatergic and GABAergic markers.
evaluation: All reviewers accept this anatomical characterization without question. Reviewer 2 explicitly states the study provides 'compelling evidence at the anatomical and physiological levels,' and the editor notes the study uses 'complementary electrophysiological and anatomical experimental approaches' that are convincing.

result: Both EPSCs and IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses exhibited paired-pulse depression, but EPSCs showed significantly stronger depression (PPR 0.46 ± 0.03) than IPSCs (PPR 0.6 ± 0.03). This differential PPR was confirmed using both terminal and axon stimulation, with fiber volley recordings showing consistent presynaptic activation.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the evidence for separate vesicle pools. Reviewer 2 notes the study demonstrates 'distinct differences in paired-pulse ratio' between glutamate and GABA transmission. The control experiments (axon stimulation, fiber volleys) are not questioned.

result: Reducing extracellular Ca2+ from 2.5 to 1 mM decreased both EPSCs and IPSCs, but IPSCs showed greater reduction (58.2 ± 2.7%) than EPSCs (45.1 ± 4.1%), suggesting different Ca2+ sensitivities for glutamate and GABA release.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this as evidence for differential release properties. Reviewer 2 explicitly mentions the study found 'distinct differences in...Ca2+ sensitivity' between the two transmitters. This finding contributes to the overall conclusion about separate vesicle pools.

result: N-type Ca2+ channel blocker (ω-conotoxin-GVIA) had no effect on either EPSCs or IPSCs, while P/Q-type Ca2+ channel blocker (ω-agatoxin-IVA) suppressed both EPSCs and IPSCs to the same extent (~23-24% of baseline), indicating both transmitters rely on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question these pharmacological findings. The shared reliance on P/Q-type channels is accepted as part of the characterization of the synapse, though it does not distinguish between vesicle pools.

result: Group II mGluR agonist DCG-IV inhibited EPSCs (IC50=0.11 μM) more than IPSCs (IC50=0.27 μM), and GABAB receptor agonist baclofen suppressed EPSCs (51.6 ± 2.4%) more than IPSCs (38.6 ± 4.3%), showing differential presynaptic receptor modulation.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this as evidence for differential release properties. Reviewer 2 notes the study demonstrates 'distinct differences in...presynaptic receptor modulation' between glutamate and GABA transmission.

result: Fast Ca2+ chelator BAPTA-AM suppressed both EPSCs and IPSCs equally, while slow chelator EGTA-AM suppressed EPSCs but not IPSCs, indicating tighter spatial coupling between Ca2+ channels and synaptic vesicles for GABA release than for glutamate release.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this as key evidence for separate vesicle pools with different spatial arrangements. Reviewer 2 explicitly mentions 'distinct...Ca2+ channel-vesicle coupling configuration for each neurotransmitter.' This is treated as strong evidence for the main conclusion.

result: Minimal light stimulation experiments detected predominantly independent EPSC-only (5.1 ± 0.5% probability) and IPSC-only (3.9 ± 0.4% probability) responses, with biphasic responses being rare (1.1 ± 0.3% probability). Pharmacological controls confirmed these responses were not contaminated, and amplitude analysis suggested unitary vesicle release.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these minimal stimulation findings as evidence for independent release sites. Reviewer 2 notes the study shows 'glutamate/GABA co-release produces independent glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic responses.' The controls are not questioned.

result: Strontium-induced asynchronous release experiments showed that the majority of events were EPSC-only (27.9 ± 4.7) or IPSC-only (23.4 ± 4.2), with biphasic events being rare (2.5 ± 0.5), confirming independent release of glutamate and GABA.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this as complementary evidence for independent release. The strontium experiments are not specifically critiqued and support the same conclusion as the minimal stimulation experiments.

result: Electron microscopy showed that SuM terminals formed both asymmetric (excitatory) and symmetric (inhibitory) synapses, with single terminals forming both types. Immunofluorescence revealed that 52.5% of VGluT2-positive terminals were associated with both GluN1 and GABAAα1 receptors at an average distance of 397.5 ± 8.75 nm, indicating segregated postsynaptic targets.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these anatomical findings as evidence for segregated synapses from the same terminal. Reviewer 2 notes 'most SuM boutons form distinct glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses at proximity' and that the study shows 'segregated postsynaptic targets.' The editor describes this as 'convincing evidence.'

result: Retrograde tracing with fluorescent microspheres injected into the dorsal DG did not reveal any retrogradely labeled neurons in the VTA, while labeled neurons were observed in the SuM and entorhinal cortex.
evaluation: This control experiment is not questioned by reviewers. It serves to rule out VTA as a source of the observed co-transmission in the DG.

result: Train stimulation at 5, 10, and 20 Hz revealed that EPSCs showed frequency-dependent depression (stronger at higher frequencies), while IPSCs showed frequency-independent stable depression. At 10 and 20 Hz, EPSC depression was significantly stronger than IPSC depression, with fiber volley recordings confirming consistent presynaptic activation.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as evidence for distinct short-term plasticity. Reviewer 2 explicitly states the study demonstrates 'glutamate/GABA co-transmission exhibits distinct short-term plasticity, with glutamate showing frequency-dependent depression and GABA showing frequency-independent stable depression.'

result: Pharmacological experiments ruled out postsynaptic receptor saturation/desensitization as the mechanism of short-term depression. γDGG did not affect EPSC depression, and TPMPA did not affect IPSC depression, suggesting presynaptic origins.
evaluation: These control experiments are not questioned by reviewers and support the interpretation that the observed plasticity is presynaptic in origin.

result: At 5 Hz, SuM activation enhanced granule cell firing throughout the train, with further enhancement when GABAergic transmission was blocked. At higher frequencies (10 and 20 Hz), the excitatory effect was attenuated and disappeared in later stimulations, but blocking GABAergic transmission with picrotoxin restored the excitatory effect, demonstrating frequency-dependent filtering.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these functional findings as demonstrating the physiological consequences of the distinct transmission modes. The editor notes the study provides 'convincing evidence that the co-release of glutamate and GABA from different vesicles within the same terminal could modulate granule cell firing in a frequency-dependent manner.'

result: The authors conclude that glutamate and GABA are co-released from different synaptic vesicles within SuM terminals, and that distinct transmission modes of glutamate/GABA co-release serve as frequency-dependent filters of SuM inputs.
evaluation: All reviewers accept this main conclusion. The editor states the work provides 'convincing evidence that the co-release of glutamate and GABA from different vesicles within the same terminal could modulate granule cell firing in a frequency-dependent manner.' Reviewer 1 notes 'I came away believing that the boutons may indeed produce and release distinct types of vesicles,' though adds 'the strength of the conclusion rests on the abundance of data (approaches) rather than the decisiveness of any one approach.' Reviewer 2 states the authors 'provide compelling evidence...that glutamate and GABA are co-release by different synaptic vesicles.'
